extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers who want to write characters outside their own culture or lived experience
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft and industry guidance for authors who want to write characters whose cultural identities differ from their own, focused on research, characterization, and how to present work to agents/editors. Emphasizes due diligence, specificity, sensitivity readers, and ethical amplification of own-voices creators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the work / do the research / do your due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: You must put in the work: research the culture/identity you are writing, read widely, take classes, consult resources such as Writing the Other, and prepare before claiming to represent someone else's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recommended actions include reading books (fiction, nonfiction, and children's books), taking classes, visiting writingtheother.com, and otherwise building a foundation of knowledge before or during drafting. The hosts repeatedly stress that this is foundational to producing good representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show that you've done your homework
rubrics_metrics.description: When presenting work to agents/editors (or critics), be ready to demonstrate the specific research and steps you've taken to get the representation right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a list of things you did or will do: books read, people interviewed, classes taken, sensitivity readers hired. Present this list proactively to agents/editors to alleviate their fears and show you took due diligence seriously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get feedback from people who share the identity (sensitivity/alpha readers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have people from that culture read your draft and give feedback; be willing to hire sensitivity readers and to learn from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensitivity readers and culture-specific readers are recommended, but the hosts warn this is not a 'magical rubberstamp' that guarantees immunity from criticism. Use feedback to revise; be open to correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a specific, fully realized person — avoid 'stand-in' characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't write a character who functions as a generic stand-in for an entire culture or identity; instead, give specificity (place, neighborhood, family history, interior life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the character like any good well-developed character: age, gender, region, family background, history, and particularities. Specificity and intersectionality help prevent flat or stereotyped portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotypes and simplistic representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad representation often looks like lazy or bad writing — relying on clichés, tropes, or presenting the character as representative of all people with that identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weed out clichés during revision; ensure characters aren't reduced to a single trait or cultural shorthand. Invest details and nuance to counter stereotypical depictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and deeply — including targeted magazines and many books
rubrics_metrics.description: Immerse yourself in literature and media produced for and by the community you're representing; read broadly across fiction, nonfiction, and children's books to understand cultural textures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestions include reading magazines aimed at that group, and an oft-cited heuristic: 'read a hundred books' across genres and formats to build context and sensitivity. Children's books are useful for understanding cultural transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for criticism — do the work but accept you may still be called out
rubrics_metrics.description: Even with diligent research and sensitivity readers, criticism can and will happen; be ready to 'take your lumps' and respond constructively rather than expecting immunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand there is no protection from all criticism; treat feedback as part of the process. The hosts emphasize humility and readiness to learn rather than defensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your privilege to lift up own-voices authors (don't monopolize space)
rubrics_metrics.description: When researching and publishing, actively promote and amplify authors from the identity you're writing — introduce them to agents/editors, retweet, recommend, and otherwise increase their visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions include recommending researched authors to your network, introducing them to industry contacts, and using platform/privilege to expand opportunities rather than solely profiting from others' stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and communicate remediation steps to industry stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agent or editor expresses fear about a manuscript, alleviate concern by documenting research steps and offering concrete remediation such as hiring sensitivity readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be proactive in communicating the work you've done and the steps you're willing to take. This reduces fear among decision-makers and shows you will collaborate to get representation right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist the 'default' — include diverse characters intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: The default tendency to write characters only like oneself perpetuates lack of representation; consciously include diverse, intersectional characters to reflect the real world's complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't be paralyzed by fear; inclusion requires effort. Intentionally represent people from various cultures and marginalizations in nuanced ways as part of resisting the default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with nuance and allow for complex receptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for nuanced portrayals that may still provoke diverse reactions — accept that works can be both beloved and critiqued simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages a nuanced public conversation: call out actively harmful depictions while recognizing that well-intentioned, complex works can still be loved by many. Strive for nuance in both creation and response to critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand that bad representation often signals craft problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor representation frequently stems from general weaknesses in characterization and craft, not merely the author's identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on overall craft — interiority, specificity, plotting — because strong writing reduces the risk of representations reading as flat or offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-level remedy: increase diversity within publishing decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: A structural solution is to increase diversity among agents, editors, and other publishing gatekeepers so informed decisions about representation can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hosts note that a lack of diverse decision-makers amplifies fear and mistakes; long-term improvement requires changing who is in positions of authority inside publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat research as iterative; be willing to revise or do more work
rubrics_metrics.description: Research and remedial steps are not one-off; be ready to realize mid-process that you need to read more, interview more people, or change aspects of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the homework list, then use it to identify gaps. If you discover weaknesses during preparation, return to research and revise rather than pushing an insufficient draft forward.
